replies.author: Poietilinx
replies.body:
How did you made it? its really cool.  
Gerstner's waves is this algorithm here  
[https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems/part-i-natural-effects/chapter-1-effective-water-simulation-physical-models](https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems/part-i-natural-effects/chapter-1-effective-water-simulation-physical-models)

The overall idea is that you create a wavefront of sines and you set them to clash against each other at different speeds and lengths and heights on a 3d plane.

The vertex manipulation part of it toddlers level math level to implement, but the reconstruction of the normals and binormals (so you can calculate light with it) its quite a pain. Cuz the waves are built by an superposition of waves you have use partial derivatives to rebuilt them) but then again... I think with ai, it wouldnt be that hard to implement you can literally point to that page and it will write the algorithm for you in a file xD

thats an old algorithm, most games use it or a variation of it, there are some really good presentations from some game studios you can watch to see stuff they have done to make it look better.

replies.author: Poietilinx
replies.body:
hum.. ther's a math to build those cell style noise, how was it again?  
yeah there was a book with that info  
[https://thebookofshaders.com/12/](https://thebookofshaders.com/12/)  
its not complex stuff in the slightest, you just divide the space by how many cells you want, then you normalize whatever noise function you wrote to that cell size value. then you "move the cell" back to where that tile is.
